summary:
**Flame in Freefall** is an offline-first web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It transforms NASA research on fire behavior in microgravity into accessible, evidence-based information to support astronaut safety during space missions.

The platform features verified evidence cards extracted from NASA research papers, ranked according to their relevance to crew safety. It also includes an AI-powered Ask page, allowing users to ask questions and receive answers grounded in scientific evidence through a locally running language model, without relying on cloud services or an internet connection. A dedicated page highlights what NASA still doesn't know about fire in space, making research gaps visible rather than presenting scientific knowledge as complete.

To ensure reliability, we developed a research-to-evidence pipeline that extracts scientific papers, generates draft cards, validates them, and requires human review before any evidence is published. The project combines AI with human verification to reduce misinformation and make complex scientific research easier to understand.

By turning scattered research into an accessible, traceable, and fully offline knowledge tool, Flame in Freefall helps bridge the gap between scientific discovery and practical crew safety.
details:
What it does / how it works Flame in Freefall turns NASA fire-in-space research (SAFFIRE, FLEX, BASS-II) into 31 evidence cards. Each card holds one finding, its exact quote, its PDF page and its numbers as written.

Pipeline: NASA PDF → text extracted page by page → card draft → automatic check that the quote and every number appear word for word on the stated page → team acceptance → app. Only accepted cards are shown.

The app runs fully offline on one laptop:

Explore: filter the cards by hazard, control type and material, and rank them with crew-safety / evidence / Moon-Mars sliders. A stability badge shows which cards stay in the top 10 whatever the weighting.

Card pages: NASA's quote, page and values, plus trust badges showing what was checked.

Ask: a local AI (Ollama) answers only from the matching cards and must cite them. When our cards don't cover a question, it says "Not in our evidence". If the AI is off, checked pre-written answers are shown.

What NASA doesn't know: open questions stated in the sources, gaps in our evidence, and cards that conflict.

Earth vs Space, Data and Method pages.

Every piece of content is labelled with its layer: NASA found (blue), our safety reading (orange), AI explanation (purple).

Benefits Planners, crews and students can see in seconds what NASA actually found about fire in space, with the source page. Interpretation is never mixed with evidence. The app works without internet, as it would have to in a habitat or spacecraft.

Intended impact Safer material choices and fire procedures for Moon and Mars missions. Key findings include:

NASA's Earth flammability test is not conservative.

Nitrogen jets can strengthen a flame in microgravity.

Invisible cool flames can keep burning after the visible flame is out.

The app also gives a clear list of what NASA says is still unknown, to guide the next experiments.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

App: TypeScript, Next.js (React), Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Ajv, Vitest.

Pipeline: Python with pdfplumber, rapidfuzz and jsonschema.

AI in the app: Ollama with Llama 3.1 8B, run locally.

Development: GitHub with GitHub Actions CI. Claude (Anthropic) via Claude Code helped write code, tests and documentation, and drafted the cards from the NASA texts.

Hardware: a standard laptop; no cloud services at runtime.

Creativity Every claim is verifiable: an automatic check rejects any quote or number not found on its page. The three colour-coded layers separate NASA's findings from our reading and from AI text. Ranking stability is tested across 27 weightings. A "what NASA doesn't know" view turns open questions into a research agenda. And the local AI can only answer from evidence, or say it can't.

Factors considered

Accuracy and honesty: no invented data, AI never shown as NASA guidance, and how each card was checked shown openly.

Offline use and crew safety relevance.

Accessibility: text labels, never colour alone.

Projector and laptop readability.

Transparency: the method, the AI prompt and the sources are all public in the app.

AI disclosure: the cards were drafted by Claude and checked automatically, word for word, against the NASA pages. The team accepted them on that basis.
